question: On 29 September, Commissioner McGrath visited Poland. The Commissioner said the visit began with a ‘valuable discussion’ with Minister Żurek on justice reform and EU cooperation1. Three days after the meeting, Minister Żurek decided, in breach of the Constitution and the law, to restore the manual assignment of cases, departing from the statutory principle of panels of judges being drawn by lots2.

He also published a draft bill on ‘infected’ courts, using totalitarian vocabulary and seeking to introduce segregation and verification – as was done in communist times. This is a clear example of an ostentatious return to manual control of the courts.

These issues, together with the attempt to abolish the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau and the scandals over the dismissal of corruption cases involving very close colleagues of Tusk,3 have provoked outrage in Poland. In connection with this flagrant attack on the independence of the judiciary, the National Judicial Council has accused Minister Żurek of breaching the Constitution4.

The President5 and a range of legal authorities take a similar view6. The Commissioner for Human Rights has said that any changes to the way judges are assigned should be made by law7. Meanwhile, Commissioner McGrath, hiding behind the façade of phrases and successful dialogue, is taking part in the destruction of the rule of law under Tusk’s authority. 1.

Was Commissioner McGrath consulted during his meeting with Minister Żurek on the draft regulation on de facto abolishing the process of drawing lots for judges and the restoration of manual control of courts, the abolition of the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau and the segregation of judges?

Is the Commission aware that in recent months there has been a drastic fall in trust in the courts8, and that Minister Żurek, as a symbol of the deterioration of the justice system, is further exacerbating this crisis?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2025) The Commission is aware of the draft Regulation amending the rules on the assignment of cases to judges and is currently assessing it. It was not discussed by the Commissioner responsible for democracy, justice, the rule of law and consumer protection and the Polish Minister of Justice at their meeting of 29 September 2025.

On the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau, the Commission reported on plans to transfer it to the police and reinforce it, in its 2025 Rule of Law Report country chapter for Poland. The Commission also reported on issues pertaining to the effectiveness of the justice system in Poland and on efforts made to advance on the implementation of the Action Plan on the Rule of Law.
Recommendations were made to Poland in this respect. The Commission will continue to monitor the Polish government actions aimed at restoring the rule of law.
